title: AT&T Swapped Its Scoreboard For A Forecast
detail:
AT&T Swapped Its Scoreboard For A Forecast
Trefis Team
Thu, July 30, 2026 at 10:06 AM PDT 4 min read
T
T-PA
CHTR
TMUS
VZ
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by TheDigitalArtist on Pixabay

The company still reports the numbers it used to lead with, but the case out front now rests on a payoff much further away.

The Story Used To Be Counted Product By Product

If you have held AT&T (T) a couple of years, the story you bought was a build with a scoreboard attached. Roughly two years ago the ambition was stated plainly: "lead the industry in converged connectivity through 5G and fiber." The proof came product by product, countable: 403,000 postpaid phone net adds in a third quarter, and more than 200,000 AT&T Fiber net adds. The 5G and fiber investment was described then as fueling growth already, not as a later payoff.

Now The Strategic Case Leans On A Traffic Forecast For 2035

The front of the story looks different today. The lead customer figure is a single blended one, more than 1 million Advanced Connectivity subscribers gained across fiber, fixed wireless and postpaid phones, and the strategic case rests on AI. Management's framing is that agentic AI is reshaping network traffic, citing industry research that AI agents can generate up to 450% more total traffic per task than a human doing the same work, plus projections of roughly 9X growth in enterprise traffic and 7X growth in consumer traffic by 2035.

The asset did not change; the reason to own it did. The same Advanced Connectivity operation now pitched on future traffic already supplies more than 90% of service revenue and nearly all adjusted EBITDA. In the reported financials, trailing twelve-month revenue is about $127 billion and the Communications segment alone runs near $120.9 billion, about 95% of the total. No revenue line sits beside the AI case, only traffic multiples and a horizon no quarterly report can settle.

What The Blended Number Cannot Show You About Fiber ARPU

The business that used to be the headline is not soft, which makes this a pivot rather than a retreat. Revenue over the last twelve months is up 2.6% year over year, against a three-year average pace of 1.6%. Net margin of 16.9% sits well above its 10.8% three-year average and close to its 17.9% three-year peak. Advanced Connectivity service revenue grew 5.1% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, and the consolidated adjusted EBITDA margin rose 110 basis points to 39%, the highest the company says it has recorded since it refocused the business on Advanced Connectivity.

One metric does sit underneath the new frame. Fiber ARPU fell 1.3% from a year earlier, and excluding the footprint acquired from Lumen it was roughly flat. Management says that is a choice: the goal is to maximize total Advanced Connectivity service revenue rather than the ARPU of any single product, and it expects convergence to keep some pressure on Fiber ARPU in the near term. The CFO has also allowed that broadband revenue may come in a little below what the company guided, with wireless a little above.

title: The Number That Could Keep Verizon Communications Stock Climbing
detail:
The Number That Could Keep Verizon Communications Stock Climbing
Trefis Team
Thu, July 30, 2026 at 8:27 AM PDT 4 min read
VZ
^GSPC
CMCSA
TMUS
T
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by geralt on Pixabay

A falling churn rate is quietly doing more for Verizon than any headline contract, and it is why management keeps raising its own guidance.

The Stock Paused While The Business Sped Up

Verizon Communications (VZ) stock has returned about 24% over the past six months and trades around 5% below its 52-week high. The odd part is the past three months, when it returned just 1.7% against 2.5% for the S&P 500. The stock went quiet in exactly the stretch when the operating numbers did the opposite.

The Churn Number Behind The Guidance Raises

Consumer postpaid phone churn ran 95 basis points in the fourth quarter of 2025, 90 basis points in the first quarter of 2026, and 84 basis points in the second. That reverses several years of churn pushing the other way, and it rewrites the economics of every customer added. Management, hardly a neutral witness, calls it a step change.

The part that gets missed: Verizon is adding more customers while paying less to get them. Postpaid phone net additions went from 55,000 in the first quarter of 2026 to 184,000 in the second, putting the first half 537,000 ahead of a year earlier, and by the company's own account, the promotional cost of acquiring a consumer improved about 15% year over year in that quarter, while the promotional cost of retention improved about 17%.

That is why the guidance keeps moving. Adjusted earnings-per-share growth guidance for 2026 started at 4% to 5%, was raised to 5% to 6%, and now stands at 6% to 7%. Free cash flow growth guidance went from roughly 7% or better to 9% to 10%, and first-half free cash flow reached $10.2 billion, up 16%. Over the prior five years, free cash flow and adjusted earnings per share both grew at roughly negative 1% a year. The catch is what Verizon gave up to buy that loyalty.

Can A Simpler Price Plan Pay For Itself?

By its own description, Verizon scrapped activation and upgrade fees, added monthly cash back, and separated phone subsidies from the price of the plan. The fees and the cash back are real money going away.

Its answer is volume and mix instead of price, and so far it is working. Mobility and broadband service revenue growth went from 1.6% in the first quarter of 2026 to 2.8% in the second; the full-year guide moved up to 2.5% to 3%, and management now expects approximately 4% year-over-year growth in the fourth quarter of 2026. There is room to recover: reported operating margin over the trailing twelve months, at 21%, sits below its three-year peak of 23%, and total revenue is growing four times its three-year average pace of 0.7%.

title: Does AT&T Stock Actually Diversify Your Portfolio?

Does AT&T Stock Actually Diversify Your Portfolio?

Explore stocks on Coinbase

Photo by Mohamed_hassan on Pixabay

Its five-year correlation to the index is low enough that most of its return has been its own story, and over the past year it has tended to move opposite the market.

AT&T (T) stock was up nearly 11% over the course of a week before correcting nearly 3% yesterday. On the other hand, S&P 500 is down over the same stretch, a window that also takes in AT&T's June-quarter results. A holding that rises while the index falls is tempting, but one week of prices proves nothing about how a stock behaves. The question that decides what this position does to your money is how much of its return is genuinely its own rather than the market you already own through an index fund and what it does to the swings in everything else.

What A Correlation Of 0.18 Actually Buys You

Over the past five years AT&T stock has carried a correlation to the S&P 500 of 0.18. A reading of 1.0 would mean perfect lockstep with the index; 0 would mean unrelated moves. At 0.18, most of what these shares have done has been their own story, which is the defining trait of a genuine portfolio diversifier. It compounded while doing it, at 9.2% a year over that five-year window against 12.7% for the S&P 500, and at an annualized volatility of 25% versus 17.1% for the index. Over those same five years the two assets people reach for instead did this: gold returned 17.0% a year at a correlation to AT&T of just 0.03, while the VNQ real estate index returned 2.9% at a correlation of 0.34. Gold did better on both counts over that stretch; the point is that this stock is a third, largely independent return stream, not a substitute for either.

AT&T Fell On The Market's Good Days And Rose On Its Bad Ones

The capture readings show how that independence feels. Over the past year, for every move up in the S&P 500, AT&T moved about 51% in the opposite direction, tending to fall when the market rose. For every move down in the index, it moved about 55% in the opposite direction, tending to rise. That is counter-cyclical behavior, not a quiet stock: it leans against the market rather than sitting still through it. The stock has fallen more than 10% over the past twelve months and sits about > 15% below its 52-week high. This is a one-year reading, and it can shift; behind it is a business mid-transition.

Subscriber Volumes Are Up, Fiber Pricing Is Under Pressure

In the June 2026 quarter AT&T grew service revenue 2.7% year over year and lifted adjusted EBITDA 5.2%, with a 39% adjusted EBITDA margin, and it added more than 1 million Advanced Connectivity subscribers across fiber, fixed wireless, and postpaid phones. Management raised the planned 2026 buyback by up to 25%, to roughly $10 billion, saying it sees a gap between the business and the stock's valuation; the shares trade at 7.9 times earnings against an S&P 500 median of 24.4. The bear case sits in the same results: fiber ARPU fell 1.3% year over year, and was only flat excluding the lower-ARPU Lumen footprint; management says convergence will likely keep pressure on it in the near term. Leverage is the other open item, at 2.68 times adjusted EBITDA and expected to rise to around 3.2 times once the EchoStar spectrum purchase closes.

Verizon Traded Phone Upgrades For Cash Flow

VZ

Photo by wynpnt on Pixabay

The revenue shortfall and the record margin came out of the same decision, and management raised its full-year outlook on the strength of it.

Why Did A $2 Billion Revenue Miss Send The Stock Up 5.8%?

Verizon Communications (VZ) reported Q2 FY2026 revenue of $34.25 billion against a consensus estimate of $36.21 billion, a shortfall of nearly $2 billion. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $1.30, up 6.6% year over year and ahead of the $1.27 to $1.28 analysts expected. Neither line explains what happened next: the stock rose 5.8% on the day it reported, July 24.

The number that mattered sat further down: mobility and broadband service revenue grew 2.8% year over year, up from 1.6% in Q1 FY2026. That acceleration is why management lifted its full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guide to a range of $4.95 to $4.99 from a prior $4.92. What moved was the outlook, and the revenue Verizon gave up was revenue it chose to give up.

The Upgrade Volumes Verizon Cut By Nearly 27%

The company is pulling phone subsidies out of its wireless pricing, a change it says means meaningfully better margins. Upgrade volumes fell nearly 27% from a year earlier, and equipment revenue dropped nearly 20%, more than $1.2 billion. The service lines grew, so the weakness sat on the side of the business Verizon is trying to make smaller.

What that bought was operating leverage. Adjusted EBITDA reached $13.7 billion, up 7.2%, at a 40% margin management calls the highest it has ever reported, and free cash flow was $6.4 billion, up 24% from a year earlier. Over the prior five years, by management's own account, average annual growth in free cash flow and adjusted EPS ran at roughly negative 1%. Whether the improvement repeats turns on one metric.

Is 84 Basis Points Of Churn A Turn Or One Good Quarter?

The leading indicators argue for the former. Consumer postpaid phone churn was 84 basis points, down from 90 basis points in Q1 2026 and 6 basis points better than a year earlier. Verizon posted 184,000 postpaid phone net additions, a 193,000 swing from a year earlier, and 348,000 broadband net additions on a base of over 17.1 million. Management says its consumer promotional cost of acquisition improved about 15% year over year while cost of retention improved about 17%.

Winning customers more cheaply and losing fewer of them is the whole mechanism, and the company now expects mobility and broadband service revenue to approach 3% growth in Q3 2026 and about 4% in Q4 2026. Net margin at 12.5% sits above its three-year average of 11.9%, though still short of its 15.6% three-year peak. The recovery is real and it is not finished.

SpaceX is reportedly seeking spectrum better suited for urban and densely populated areas.

The company is said to be weighing acquisitions or bidding in a government spectrum auction scheduled for next year.

The move is seen as a step toward Starlink competing directly with established U.S. wireless providers.

Shares of AT&T (T), Verizon (VZ), and T-Mobile (TMUS) fell on Wednesday and ended the session lower following a report that Starlink operator SpaceX (SPCX) is seeking wireless spectrum for urban and densely populated areas. The report raised concerns that the Elon Musk-led company could compete directly with the major U.S. carriers.

While AT&T ended the session down around 3%, Verizon fell about 2%, and T-Mobile closed nearly 0.5% lower.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

SPCX Eyes Urban Spectrum

Elon Musk's SpaceX has been hunting for spectrum that works well in cities and densely populated areas as it looks to fill a gap in its airwaves needed for a full-service wireless network, Semafor reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

According to the report, the company is considering acquiring competitors to obtain the spectrum or competing in a government auction scheduled for next year. The move is a sign that SpaceX's satellite internet service, Starlink, may be preparing to compete directly with major wireless carriers such as AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile.

Spectrum Auction In Focus

Semafor reported that AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile have spent about $110 billion over the past decade acquiring much of the low-band spectrum in the U.S. That low-band spectrum, known as the C spectrum, is scheduled to be auctioned next year and has both satellite and terrestrial applications.

The report said that if SpaceX competes in the auction, it could force legacy carriers to take on unsustainable levels of debt. However, it added that SpaceX's plans remain fluid and the company could ultimately decide not to move forward.

SpaceX Lands $1.6B Space Force Contract

Separately, SpaceX won a $1.6 billion order from the U.S. Space Force on Wednesday to launch 18 Falcon 9 missions through 2027 carrying Pentagon satellites for detecting and targeting airborne objects, reported Reuters.

The missions were awarded under two task orders as part of the U.S. Space Force's flagship launch procurement program, where SpaceX, United Launch Alliance, Blue Origin and other U.S. launch providers compete for mission assignments.

Investors seeking high-reward opportunities often look toward disruptive technologies, and few names spark as much debate as AST SpaceMobile (NASDAQ:ASTS) and QuantumScape (NASDAQ:QS) as they race toward commercial scale.

AST SpaceMobile is building a satellite-to-smartphone broadband network to eliminate global connectivity gaps, while QuantumScape aims to revolutionize the electric vehicle market with safer, faster-charging solid-state batteries. Both companies are navigating the difficult transition from research and development to sustainable revenue generation.

The case for AST SpaceMobile

AST SpaceMobile aims to provide cellular broadband directly to standard smartphones without the need for specialized hardware or satellite dishes. It operates through partnerships with major mobile network operators, such as AT&T, Verizon, and Vodafone, which plan to integrate the service into their existing consumer plans. This revenue-sharing model relies on these operators offering the service to their users within the communication stocks space.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $70.9 million, representing growth of 1,511% over the previous fiscal year. The company reported a net loss of close to $341.9 million for the same period as it continued to invest in its satellite constellation. This resulted in a net margin of negative 482%

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is roughly 16.4x. This ratio measures a company's ability to cover its short-term debts with its most liquid assets. The debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.93x, representing the amount of total debt relative to shareholder equity. Free cash flow was negative $1.1 billion, which is the cash a company generates after subtracting capital expenditures from its operating cash flow.

The case for QuantumScape

QuantumScape is developing solid-state lithium-metal batteries designed to significantly improve the range and safety of electric vehicles compared to traditional battery tech. Its primary strategic partnership is with Volkswagen and its subsidiary, PowerCo, to industrialize this technology for mass production. It also maintains a multi-year partnership with Honda for further development and technology validation for future vehicle prototypes.

In FY 2025, the company reported revenue of $0.0 as it remains in the pre-commercialization stage. The net loss for the year was approximately $435.1 million, which reflects the significant investment required to test its battery cells before they reach the consumer market. This net loss is typical for companies in the industrial tech sector that are still in the heavy research and development phase.

PM guided FY2026 adjusted diluted EPS of $8.36 to $8.51, a 10.9%–12.9% jump, and targets a 9%–11% CAGR through 2028 ex-currency. IQOS reaches 108 markets, ZYN reaches 58 markets, and smoke-free is roughly 41.5% of revenue. Analyst target: $194.86.

Risk: Q1 ZYN shipments fell 23.5% on distributor destocking, and PM has paused buybacks to prioritize deleveraging. Add the Swiss withholding wrinkle for taxable-account investors.

The reason is simple: those who leave their careers to enjoy a well-deserved retirement lose the benefits of a regular salary, such as 401(k) matching and company-paid healthcare. In addition, many Boomers use their retirement years to travel and enjoy the rewards they have worked hard to achieve throughout their lives. Choosing investments wisely is imperative, and at 24/7 Wall St., we continually seek the best ideas for Baby Boomers and retirees.

One concern many Boomers and retirees have is generating enough passive income to maintain the lifestyle to which they were accustomed during their working days. One of the best ideas, and one we have championed here at 24/7 Wall St. for years, is quality high-yield dividend stocks. The problem is that many of our favorite companies have traded higher over the past few years, and the risk-reward for many has diminished. Why Do We Cover the High-Yielding Dividend Stocks?

Since 1926, dividends have accounted for approximately 32% of the S&P 500's total return, while capital appreciation has accounted for 68%. Therefore, sustainable dividend income and the potential for capital appreciation are essential to total return expectations. A study by Hartford Funds, in collaboration with Ned Davis Research, found that dividend stocks delivered an annualized return of 9.18% over the past 50 years (1973 to 2023).
